//: COPY TO tauri.release.json (gitignored) AND SET YOUR OWN DOWNLOAD HOST AND UPDATER PUBLIC KEY. Merged over tauri.conf.json at build time by scripts/tauri-build.mjs. Only the keys you override need to be here; everything else comes from tauri.conf.json.
//endpoints: This is where the DESKTOP UPDATER looks for latest.json — an installed app checks exactly this URL forever, so it must be a host you control and do not intend to rename. deploy/ops/dual-ship.sh writes latest.json (and latest-lite.json for the Lite build, whose endpoint scripts/tauri-build.mjs derives from this one) at the download host's root.
//pubkey: THE OTHER HALF OF UPDATER IDENTITY, AND A FORK MUST REPLACE IT. An installed app accepts an update only if latest.json's signature verifies against the minisign public key compiled into it. The tracked tauri.conf.json carries the ORIGINAL project's public key, so a build without this override trusts a private key you do not have: every update you sign is refused with 'update could not be installed' and the only recovery is a manual reinstall by every user. Generate your pair ONCE — `npx tauri signer generate -w ~/.puca/tauri-updater.key` — paste the printed public key here, export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY (the private file's contents) and TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD before every build, and back the private key up (deploy/ops/backup-keys.sh): losing it strands every installed client on its current version. Changing this key later is a flag day for the same reason.
//productName: USUALLY YOU DO NOT NEED THIS KEY AT ALL. On Windows, productName is not a label: NSIS derives the install directory, the Add/Remove-Programs registry key and the autostart Run value from it, and finds an existing install by looking up that uninstall key -- so a build whose productName differs from what a user already has does not find their install and puts a SECOND one beside it. frontend/src-tauri/installer-hooks.nsh solves this by detecting the OLD name's registry entry and migrating it in place before the new files are written -- tested against two real prior installs on 2026-08-25, app data and identity confirmed byte-identical before and after. If your users installed under a name other than "Sovereign", add it to the MigrateRenamedInstall call in that file rather than pinning productName here; the hook is the thing that actually gets you a real upgrade instead of a name that merely stays the same forever. Only set productName here as a manual fallback if you do not want to touch the NSIS hook -- it fully prevents the parallel-install problem but does not clean up the old one, so your users keep two copies until they remove the first by hand.
